quizzes.title: Capitals & Continents
quizzes.description: Start here: capitals, oceans and the big shapes on the map.

questions.text: What is the capital of Japan?
questions.explanation: Tokyo has been Japan's capital since 1868, when the imperial court moved there from Kyoto.

questions.text: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
questions.explanation: The Pacific covers roughly a third of Earth's surface — more than all the land combined.

questions.text: The Sahara Desert is in Africa.
questions.explanation: The Sahara stretches across much of North Africa and is the largest hot desert in the world.

questions.text: On which continent is Brazil?
questions.explanation: Brazil is the largest country in South America, covering nearly half of the continent.

questions.text: What is the capital of Italy?
questions.explanation: Rome has been Italy's capital since 1871, a decade after the country was unified.

questions.text: The Nile flows into the Mediterranean Sea.
questions.explanation: The Nile runs north through Egypt and empties into the Mediterranean through its delta near Alexandria.

questions.text: Mount Everest sits on the border between Nepal and which country?
questions.explanation: Everest's summit lies on the border between Nepal and the Tibet region of China.

questions.text: What is the capital of Egypt?
questions.explanation: Cairo, on the Nile, is Egypt's capital and its largest city.

questions.text: Canada is the largest country in the world by area.
questions.explanation: Russia is the largest, at almost twice Canada's size. Canada is second.

questions.text: How many continents are there in the model most commonly taught in English-speaking countries?
questions.explanation: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. Some countries teach fewer by joining the Americas, or Europe and Asia.

quizzes.title: Rivers & Ranges
quizzes.description: Mountains, rivers, straits and the lakes between them.

questions.text: Which mountain range runs along the western edge of South America?
questions.explanation: The Andes are the longest continental mountain range in the world, at about 7,000 km.

questions.text: Which river flows through Baghdad?
questions.explanation: Baghdad is built on the Tigris. The Euphrates runs parallel to it further west.

questions.text: The Danube flows through more countries than any other river.
questions.explanation: The Danube passes through ten countries, from Germany to Ukraine, before reaching the Black Sea.

questions.text: What is the capital of Canada?
questions.explanation: Ottawa was chosen by Queen Victoria in 1857, partly as a compromise between English- and French-speaking Canada.

questions.text: Not counting Australia, which is the largest island in the world?
questions.explanation: Greenland covers about 2.1 million km². Australia is counted as a continent rather than an island.

questions.text: Which desert covers much of southern Mongolia and northern China?
questions.explanation: The Gobi is a cold desert: winters there regularly drop below −30 °C.

questions.text: Lake Titicaca lies on the border between Peru and which country?
questions.explanation: At about 3,800 m, Titicaca is often called the highest navigable lake in the world.

questions.text: Oslo is the capital of which country?
questions.explanation: Oslo sits at the head of the Oslofjord in southern Norway.

questions.text: Istanbul is the capital of Turkey.
questions.explanation: Ankara has been Turkey's capital since 1923. Istanbul is its largest city.

questions.text: The Strait of Gibraltar separates Spain from which country?
questions.explanation: At its narrowest the strait is about 14 km wide, between Europe and Africa.

quizzes.title: Borders & Islands
quizzes.description: Neighbours, coastlines and the places that are easy to mix up.

questions.text: Which country has the longest coastline in the world?
questions.explanation: Counting its thousands of Arctic islands, Canada's coastline is over 200,000 km long.

questions.text: What is the capital of Australia?
questions.explanation: Canberra was purpose-built as the capital, as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne.

questions.text: Which of these South American countries is landlocked?
questions.explanation: Bolivia lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884).

questions.text: Which is the largest country in Africa by area?
questions.explanation: Algeria became Africa's largest country in 2011, when South Sudan split from Sudan.

questions.text: The Caspian Sea is the largest lake in the world by surface area.
questions.explanation: Despite its name, the Caspian is usually classed as a lake. It covers about 370,000 km² and borders five countries.

questions.text: Which strait separates Asia from North America?
questions.explanation: The Bering Strait between Russia and Alaska is about 82 km wide at its narrowest.

questions.text: Apart from Vatican City, which independent country is completely surrounded by Italy?
questions.explanation: San Marino, on Mount Titano, is one of the oldest surviving republics in the world.

questions.text: Which is the longest river in Europe?
questions.explanation: The Volga runs about 3,500 km through Russia to the Caspian Sea. The Danube is second.

questions.text: In which country is Mount Kilimanjaro?
questions.explanation: Kilimanjaro is in northern Tanzania, close to the Kenyan border — which is why Kenya is the usual wrong answer.

questions.text: Lesotho is completely surrounded by South Africa.
questions.explanation: Lesotho is one of only three countries entirely surrounded by another, with San Marino and Vatican City.

quizzes.title: Map Masters
quizzes.description: For people who read atlases for fun.

questions.text: Which of these capital cities lies furthest north?
questions.explanation: Reykjavík is at about 64°N — the northernmost capital of a sovereign state. Helsinki, Oslo and Tallinn are all near 60°N.

questions.text: Which African river crosses the equator twice?
questions.explanation: The Congo's great arc takes it north across the equator and back south again on its way to the Atlantic.

questions.text: Which of these countries does NOT border Brazil?
questions.explanation: Chile and Ecuador are the only South American countries that don't share a border with Brazil.

questions.text: The Atacama Desert lies mainly in which country?
questions.explanation: The Atacama, in northern Chile, is one of the driest places on Earth.

questions.text: What is the capital of Bhutan?
questions.explanation: Thimphu is one of the few capital cities in the world without traffic lights.

questions.text: Which is the largest country lying entirely within Europe?
questions.explanation: Ukraine covers about 600,000 km². Russia is larger but spans Europe and Asia.

questions.text: What is the deepest lake in the world?
questions.explanation: Lake Baikal in Siberia is over 1,600 m deep and holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water.

questions.text: How many countries share a land border with Germany?
questions.explanation: Denmark, Poland, Czechia, Austria, Switzerland, France, Luxembourg, Belgium and the Netherlands.

questions.text: The Strait of Malacca separates the Malay Peninsula from which island?
questions.explanation: The Strait of Malacca is one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world.

questions.text: Which is the only country whose national flag is not a rectangle?
questions.explanation: Nepal's flag is made of two stacked triangular pennants, bordered in blue.

quizzes.title: Everyday Know-How
quizzes.description: The things everyone half-remembers from school.

questions.text: How many days are there in a leap year?
questions.explanation: A leap year adds 29 February, almost every four years, to keep the calendar in step with Earth's orbit.

questions.text: How many sides does a hexagon have?
questions.explanation: 'Hex' comes from the Greek for six — think of the cells in a honeycomb.

questions.text: A dozen means twelve.
questions.explanation: A dozen is twelve; a 'baker's dozen' is thirteen.

questions.text: What colour do you get by mixing blue and yellow paint?
questions.explanation: Blue and yellow paint make green. Red and blue make purple; red and yellow make orange.

questions.text: Which instrument has 88 keys on a standard modern model?
questions.explanation: A standard modern piano has 52 white keys and 36 black ones.

questions.text: The Summer Olympic Games are normally held every four years.
questions.explanation: The Summer and Winter Games each come round every four years, two years apart. Tokyo 2020 was the rare exception, held in 2021.

questions.text: In which country did the ancient Olympic Games begin?
questions.explanation: The ancient Games were held at Olympia, in Greece, from the 8th century BC.

questions.text: How many minutes are there in two hours?
questions.explanation: Sixty minutes an hour, times two.

questions.text: A spider has six legs.
questions.explanation: Spiders have eight legs. Insects have six — spiders aren't insects.

questions.text: Which language has the most native speakers in the world?
questions.explanation: Mandarin has the most native speakers. English has the most speakers overall once second-language speakers are counted.

quizzes.title: Pub Quiz Classics
quizzes.description: The questions that turn up at every quiz night.

questions.text: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.explanation: Leonardo began it around 1503. Today it hangs in the Louvre in Paris.

questions.text: Who wrote 'Romeo and Juliet'?
questions.explanation: Shakespeare wrote it in the mid-1590s, early in his career.

questions.text: In chess, the bishop can only move diagonally.
questions.explanation: A bishop moves any number of squares diagonally, so it stays on squares of one colour for the whole game.

questions.text: What is the currency of Japan?
questions.explanation: The yen. The won is South Korea's currency and the yuan is China's.

questions.text: How many players does a football (soccer) team have on the pitch at once?
questions.explanation: Eleven, including the goalkeeper.

questions.text: Who composed the 'Moonlight Sonata'?
questions.explanation: Beethoven wrote it in 1801. The nickname 'Moonlight' was given by a critic after his death.

questions.text: In Greek mythology, who is the king of the gods?
questions.explanation: Zeus ruled from Mount Olympus. His Roman counterpart is Jupiter.

questions.text: In which city are the headquarters of the United Nations?
questions.explanation: The UN headquarters is in New York. Geneva hosts its largest office outside it.

questions.text: 'Hola' is Italian for 'hello'.
questions.explanation: 'Hola' is Spanish. In Italian you'd say 'ciao' or 'buongiorno'.

questions.text: How many strings does a standard violin have?
questions.explanation: Four, tuned G, D, A and E.

quizzes.title: Curious Facts
quizzes.description: Trivia with a twist — the answers you'd swear were different.

questions.text: Which is the only letter that doesn't appear in any U.S. state name?
questions.explanation: J is in New Jersey, X in Texas and Z in Arizona — but no state name contains a Q.

questions.text: The Great Wall of China can be seen from the Moon with the naked eye.
questions.explanation: It's far too narrow to see from the Moon — Apollo astronauts confirmed it. It is hard to spot even from low orbit.

questions.text: Which author created the detective Hercule Poirot?
questions.explanation: Poirot first appeared in 'The Mysterious Affair at Styles' (1920). Conan Doyle created Sherlock Holmes.

questions.text: Who painted 'The Persistence of Memory', with its melting clocks?
questions.explanation: Dalí painted it in 1931. All four were surrealists, which is what makes this one tricky.

questions.text: Botanically, bananas are berries.
questions.explanation: A banana grows from a single flower with one ovary — the botanical definition of a berry. Strawberries, oddly, aren't.

questions.text: How many players are on the field for each team in rugby union?
questions.explanation: Rugby union has 15 a side. Rugby league has 13.

questions.text: In which city were the first modern Olympic Games held, in 1896?
questions.explanation: The 1896 Games were held in Athens, honouring the ancient Games' Greek origins.

questions.text: Who composed the opera 'La traviata'?
questions.explanation: Verdi's 'La traviata' premiered in Venice in 1853.

questions.text: What is the collective noun for a group of crows?
questions.explanation: A murder of crows. A parliament is owls, and both an unkindness and a conspiracy are ravens.

questions.text: How many sides does a dodecagon have?
questions.explanation: 'Dodeca' is Greek for twelve.

quizzes.title: Polymath
quizzes.description: Books, music, art and ideas — for the all-rounder.

questions.text: Which philosopher wrote 'The Republic'?
questions.explanation: Plato wrote it around 375 BC. Socrates is its main speaker but wrote nothing himself.

questions.text: Which Russian author wrote 'War and Peace'?
questions.explanation: Tolstoy published it in instalments between 1865 and 1869.

questions.text: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.explanation: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and a third pumps it round the body.

questions.text: Which novel begins with the line 'Call me Ishmael.'?
options: The Old Man and the Sea
questions.explanation: Herman Melville's 'Moby-Dick' was published in 1851.

questions.text: How many semitones are there in an octave?
questions.explanation: An octave spans twelve semitones — every key, white and black, from one C to the next.

questions.text: In which museum is the Rosetta Stone displayed?
questions.explanation: It has been in the British Museum in London since 1802.

questions.text: Which painter cut off part of his own ear in 1888?
questions.explanation: Van Gogh did it in Arles in December 1888, after a quarrel with Paul Gauguin.

questions.text: In which athletics event would you perform the 'Fosbury Flop'?
questions.explanation: Dick Fosbury won Olympic gold with the backwards technique in 1968; nearly every high jumper now uses it.

questions.text: What is the currency of Switzerland?
questions.explanation: Switzerland isn't in the EU and has kept the Swiss franc.

questions.text: Which Shakespeare play features the moneylender Shylock?
questions.explanation: Shylock's demand for 'a pound of flesh' is the heart of 'The Merchant of Venice'.

quizzes.title: Science Starters
quizzes.description: Planets, plants and the basics of how things work.

questions.text: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
questions.explanation: Iron oxide — rust — in Mars's soil gives it its red colour.

questions.text: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make their food?
questions.explanation: In photosynthesis, plants turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar using sunlight, releasing oxygen.

questions.text: At sea level, water boils at 100 °C.
questions.explanation: At sea level, pure water boils at 100 °C. Higher up, where air pressure is lower, it boils at a lower temperature.

questions.text: What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.explanation: The Sun is a star. The next closest, Proxima Centauri, is over four light-years away.

questions.text: How many planets are in our Solar System?
questions.explanation: Eight. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

questions.text: Sound travels faster than light.
questions.explanation: Light is almost a million times faster — it's why you see lightning before you hear the thunder.

questions.text: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
questions.explanation: An adult heart beats around 100,000 times a day.

questions.text: What is H₂O more commonly called?
questions.explanation: Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom make a water molecule. Hydrogen peroxide is H₂O₂.

questions.text: The Moon makes its own light.
questions.explanation: Moonlight is sunlight reflected off the Moon's surface.

questions.text: Which force keeps us on the ground?
questions.explanation: Earth's gravity pulls everything towards its centre.

quizzes.title: Body & Planet
quizzes.description: How the human body and planet Earth work.

questions.text: How many bones are in the adult human body?
questions.explanation: Babies are born with around 300 bones; many fuse together as they grow.

questions.text: Which is the largest planet in the Solar System?
questions.explanation: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.

questions.text: Humans and non-avian dinosaurs lived at the same time.
questions.explanation: Non-avian dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago; modern humans appeared only about 300,000 years ago.

questions.text: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
questions.explanation: Na comes from 'natrium', its Latin name. S is sulfur.

questions.text: Which blood cells fight infection?
questions.explanation: White blood cells are the immune system's defenders. Red cells carry oxygen and platelets help blood clot.

questions.text: What is the most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air, oxygen about 21%.

questions.text: Which organ produces insulin?
questions.explanation: Insulin is made in the pancreas, by clusters of cells called the islets of Langerhans.

questions.text: At sea level, at what temperature in Fahrenheit does water boil?
questions.explanation: 212 °F, which is 100 °C. Water freezes at 32 °F.

questions.text: Venus is the hottest planet in the Solar System.
questions.explanation: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping its surface at about 465 °C — hotter than Mercury.

questions.text: What is the largest organ of the human body?
questions.explanation: Skin covers about 2 m² on an adult. The liver is the largest internal organ.

quizzes.title: Elements & Forces
quizzes.description: Atoms, particles and the physics that ties them together.

questions.text: What is the atomic number of carbon?
questions.explanation: Carbon has six protons. 12 is the mass number of its most common isotope.

questions.text: Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon.
questions.explanation: Both are made of carbon atoms, just arranged differently — a rigid 3-D lattice in diamond, sliding sheets in graphite.

questions.text: Which of these particles has a negative charge?
questions.explanation: The electron is negative. The positron is its antimatter twin with a positive charge.

questions.text: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
questions.explanation: The ohm (Ω) is named after the German physicist Georg Ohm.

questions.text: An object's mass changes when it is taken to the Moon.
questions.explanation: Its weight drops to about a sixth, because the Moon's gravity is weaker. Its mass stays the same.

questions.text: Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.explanation: Light crosses the 150 million km in about 8 minutes 20 seconds.

questions.text: What is the most common element in the universe?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen makes up roughly three-quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe.

questions.text: Which element has the chemical symbol Fe?
questions.explanation: Fe comes from 'ferrum', the Latin for iron. Fluorine is F.

questions.text: Which planet has the shortest year?
questions.explanation: Mercury orbits the Sun in about 88 Earth days.

questions.text: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
questions.explanation: Au comes from 'aurum', the Latin for gold.

quizzes.title: Lab Legends
quizzes.description: Deep cuts from physics, chemistry, biology and space.

questions.text: What is the speed of light in a vacuum, to the nearest round figure?
questions.explanation: It's exactly 299,792.458 km/s — the metre is defined from it.

questions.text: Which scientist formulated the three laws of motion?
questions.explanation: Newton published them in his 'Principia' in 1687.

questions.text: Which of these is a noble gas?
questions.explanation: Argon is a noble gas, and it makes up almost 1% of the air.

questions.text: What is the pH of pure water at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: Pure water is neutral, with a pH of 7. Lower is acidic, higher is alkaline.

questions.text: Which part of the cell produces most of its energy, in the form of ATP?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration, and they have their own DNA.

questions.text: Who discovered penicillin in 1928?
questions.explanation: Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria on a culture plate he had left out in his London laboratory.

questions.text: What is the nearest large spiral galaxy to the Milky Way?
questions.explanation: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away, and the two galaxies are slowly moving towards each other.

questions.text: Which planet spins on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98°?
questions.explanation: Uranus was probably knocked over by a huge collision early in its history.

questions.text: What holds the two strands of a DNA double helix together?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds join the base pairs — A with T, and C with G. Weak enough to unzip when DNA is copied.

questions.text: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: One newton is the force needed to accelerate 1 kg at 1 m/s².

quizzes.title: Famous Firsts
quizzes.description: The firsts, the founders and the moments everyone knows.

questions.text: Who was the first President of the United States?
questions.explanation: Washington took office in 1789 and served two terms.

questions.text: Which ancient civilisation built the pyramids of Giza?
questions.explanation: They were built as royal tombs about 4,500 years ago.

questions.text: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon.
questions.explanation: He stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission.

questions.text: In which year did World War II end?
questions.explanation: It ended in Europe in May 1945 and in Asia in September 1945.

questions.text: Who was the first person to travel into space?
questions.explanation: Gagarin orbited Earth in Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961.

questions.text: The Titanic sank on its first voyage.
questions.explanation: It struck an iceberg on its maiden voyage in April 1912.

questions.text: In which country did the Renaissance begin?
questions.explanation: It began in Italian cities such as Florence in the 14th century.

questions.text: Which explorer reached the Americas in 1492?
questions.explanation: Columbus landed in the Bahamas, sailing for the Spanish crown.

questions.text: The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair in Paris.
questions.explanation: It was the entrance arch to the 1889 Exposition Universelle, held for the centenary of the French Revolution.

questions.text: Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?
questions.explanation: Marie Curie shared the 1903 Physics prize, and won Chemistry alone in 1911.

quizzes.title: Empires & Revolutions
quizzes.description: Rising empires, falling kings and the revolutions in between.

questions.text: In which year did the French Revolution begin?
questions.explanation: It began in 1789; the storming of the Bastille on 14 July is now France's national day.

questions.text: Who was crowned the first Emperor of the French in 1804?
questions.explanation: Napoleon crowned himself Emperor at Notre-Dame in December 1804.

questions.text: The Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
questions.explanation: The border opened on 9 November 1989, and Germany reunified the following year.

questions.text: Which empire was founded by Genghis Khan?
questions.explanation: The Mongol Empire went on to become the largest land empire in history.

questions.text: Which Roman emperor ordered a wall built across northern Britain in AD 122?
questions.explanation: Hadrian's Wall ran about 117 km, from coast to coast.

questions.text: Which civilisation built Machu Picchu?
questions.explanation: The Inca built it in the 15th century, high in the Andes of Peru.

questions.text: Which ship carried the Pilgrims to America in 1620?
questions.explanation: The Mayflower landed near Cape Cod and its passengers founded Plymouth Colony.

questions.text: Who was the British Prime Minister for most of World War II?
questions.explanation: Churchill took over from Chamberlain in May 1940 and led until July 1945.

questions.text: The United States Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1776.
questions.explanation: The Continental Congress adopted it on 4 July 1776.

questions.text: In which year did the Ottoman Empire capture Constantinople?
questions.explanation: Sultan Mehmed II took the city in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire.

quizzes.title: Turning Points
quizzes.description: Battles, treaties and the dates that changed everything.

questions.text: In which year was the Battle of Hastings fought?
questions.explanation: William of Normandy defeated King Harold II in October 1066.

questions.text: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
questions.explanation: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC and Cleopatra died in 30 BC — about 2,500 years apart. The Moon landing came about 2,000 years after her.

questions.text: Which treaty ended World War I between the Allies and Germany?
questions.explanation: Versailles was signed with Germany in 1919. Trianon was Hungary's treaty, and Brest-Litovsk took Russia out of the war in 1918.

questions.text: Who was the last Tsar of Russia?
questions.explanation: Nicholas II abdicated in 1917 and was killed with his family in 1918.

questions.text: The Hundred Years' War lasted exactly one hundred years.
questions.explanation: It ran from 1337 to 1453 — 116 years, with long truces in between.

questions.text: In which year was Magna Carta sealed?
questions.explanation: King John sealed it at Runnymede in June 1215. It was reissued in 1216 and 1225.

questions.text: In which city was the U.S. Declaration of Independence adopted?
questions.explanation: The Continental Congress met at what is now Independence Hall in Philadelphia.

questions.text: Which Persian empire did Cyrus the Great found?
questions.explanation: Cyrus founded the Achaemenid Empire in the 6th century BC.

questions.text: Whose assassination in Sarajevo in 1914 triggered World War I?
questions.explanation: Franz Ferdinand was heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne. Franz Joseph was the Emperor, his uncle.

questions.text: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with war elephants to invade Italy?
questions.explanation: Hannibal crossed the Alps in 218 BC, during the Second Punic War.

quizzes.title: Deep Archives
quizzes.description: Ancient scripts, forgotten emperors and the fine print of history.

questions.text: In which year was Romulus Augustulus deposed, marking the end of the Western Roman Empire?
questions.explanation: Odoacer deposed him in 476. Rome was sacked by the Visigoths in 410 and the Vandals in 455.

questions.text: Which Byzantine emperor built the Hagia Sophia, completed in 537?
questions.explanation: Justinian I rebuilt it after riots destroyed the earlier church in 532.

questions.text: Who was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day, 800?
questions.explanation: Charlemagne's coronation revived the title of emperor in the West. Otto I was crowned in 962.

questions.text: Which war did the Peace of Westphalia end in 1648?
options: The War of the Spanish Succession
questions.explanation: The Thirty Years' War devastated central Europe from 1618 to 1648.

questions.text: On which ship did Charles Darwin sail around the world?
questions.explanation: Darwin's five-year voyage on the Beagle (1831–1836) gave him the observations behind his theory of evolution.

questions.text: Which dynasty built most of the Great Wall of China as it stands today?
questions.explanation: Most of the surviving brick-and-stone wall was built under the Ming (1368–1644). The Qin built earlier walls.

questions.text: Which Babylonian king issued one of the earliest written law codes?
questions.explanation: The Code of Hammurabi, from about 1750 BC, was carved on a stone stele now in the Louvre.

questions.text: The Battle of Kosovo in 1389 was fought between Serbian-led forces and which empire?
questions.explanation: Both the Serbian prince Lazar and the Ottoman sultan Murad I died in the battle.

questions.text: Which civilisation wrote in the script known as Linear B?
questions.explanation: Linear B records an early form of Greek. The older Linear A was used by the Minoans and is still undeciphered.

questions.text: The Rosetta Stone was the key to deciphering which ancient writing system?
questions.explanation: Its same text in Greek, Demotic and hieroglyphs let Jean-François Champollion crack hieroglyphs in 1822.
